title: Mantua Bore Me, Naples Holds Me: the Farm, the Road to Brundisium, and the Poem He Asked Them to Burn
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Andes, the birth on the Ides of October
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Life of Donatus and Jerome's Chronicle; the identification of Andes with modern Pietole is medieval pilgrimage tradition, not archaeology
stops.campa: In a village of the Mantuan countryside, on the fifteenth of October, a son is born to a man of small property and his wife Magia Polla. The father had come up in the world by patience: hired man to a certain Magius, an attendant on the magistrates, then his son-in-law, then owner of woodland he had bought himself and hives he kept himself. They name the boy Publius Vergilius Maro. Outside, the Mincio bends through flat country and the marsh grass grows where it has always grown. No ancient source names the farm.
suggested_refs: The hamlet of Pietole Vecchia, comune of Virgilio, traditionally identified with ancient Andes

stops.name: Andes, the laurel and the poplar
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the omens are reported only in the late-antique Life
stops.campa: His mother, carrying him, dreams she gives birth to a laurel branch, and the branch on touching the earth takes root and stands up at once a full-grown tree. At the birth a poplar shoot is planted in the local custom, and it outgrows every poplar set in that ground years before. The country people call it Virgil's tree and come to it: women with child, women newly delivered, making their vows under the branches. Two brothers are born to this house. Silo dies a child, Flaccus dies grown, and the poet will mourn him under the name Daphnis.
suggested_refs: The poplar called arbor Vergilii, venerated at Andes by pregnant and newly delivered women

stops.name: Mantua, the city he will name first in his epitaph
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the poet's own repeated naming of Mantua as his city
stops.campa: The town on the Mincio is Etruscan by origin and provincial by every Roman measure. Its name is the one he will put before Rome and before Naples when the time comes to say where he was from. In his verse he keeps it: Mantua, alas, too near unlucky Cremona. He is a boy in its territory, son of a landowner too small to matter to anyone in the capital. Cisalpine Gaul is not yet fully Italy. The men working these fields will not hold Roman citizenship as of right until he is twenty-one years old.
suggested_refs: Eclogues 9.27-28 and Georgics 2.198, the poet's own naming of Mantua

stops.name: Cremona, the boyhood and the toga virilis
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Donatus and Jerome place the ceremony on the day Lucretius died, which modern scholars read as a constructed literary succession
stops.campa: He spends his boyhood at Cremona, from the first schooling to the day of the man's toga: initia aetatis Cremonae egit usque ad virilem togam. He is fifteen when they put the plain white on him. The tradition holds that the poet Lucretius died the same day, so that the Latin hexameter passes from one hand to the other without an hour between. Nobody at Cremona records it happening. It is written down three centuries later, by men who already know what the boy in the new toga is going to become.
suggested_refs: Jerome's Chronicon entry synchronizing Lucretius's death with Virgil's assumption of the toga virilis

stops.name: Milan, the studies continued
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Life gives the stop a single clause and no date
stops.campa: From Cremona he goes on to Mediolanum, largest town of the north, for the next stage of the circuit a provincial family buys for a promising son. The Life gives it one clause: he studied here, then he went to Rome. What he read there and who taught him are not recorded. He is sixteen or seventeen, and the road south is the one his father's money expects to end in a Roman courtroom. He will be on these roads, in one direction or the other, for the next thirty-five years.
suggested_refs: The educational circuit Cremona to Milan to Rome, standard for equestrian families of Cisalpine Gaul

stops.name: Rome, rhetoric and the one case
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the curriculum rests solely on the late-antique Life, and the draft claim that he studied law has been struck
stops.campa: At Rome he studies rhetoric, and after it medicine and above all mathematics, the sciences of measure and of the stars. Epidius is named among his teachers, the same man the tradition attaches to the young Octavian. He pleads exactly one case in the courts and never pleads another: his speech is slow, his manner hesitant, and the forum rewards neither. The career an equestrian family plans for a clever son closes in a single morning, and he lets it close and does not try again.
suggested_refs: Epidius the rhetor, named by Donatus as teacher of both Virgil and Octavian

stops.name: Naples, the garden of Siro
stops.date_confidence: traditional; corroborated by poems of the Appendix Vergiliana whose attribution is itself disputed
stops.campa: He goes down to the bay and puts himself under Siro the Epicurean, and the turn is permanent. Away from the forum he takes up the doctrine of the garden: the gods do not trouble themselves about men, fear is the disease and knowledge the cure, and the good life is a small one, lived among friends and away from public business. Naples keeps him. He will live here through the Georgics and through the eleven years of the Aeneid, going up to Rome as an errand and coming back as a habit. Parthenope, he calls the city, using the older Greek name.
suggested_refs: The Catalepton poems addressed to Siro, in the Appendix Vergiliana
sources: Philodemus papyri on the circle of Siro

stops.name: Herculaneum, the library under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: scholarly reconstruction; no ancient text places Virgil or Siro's school at Herculaneum
stops.campa: Some modern scholars put Siro's school not in Naples proper but here, along the shore under Vesuvius, and point to the villa whose carbonized library, dug out of the ash seventeen centuries later, turns out to be Epicurean and full of Philodemus. The ancient Lives say only Naples. This pin is set for the argument and not for the fact. What is certain is that a school of the garden was working on this coast while Virgil was young, and that the books it read came out of the ground burnt black and legible.
suggested_refs: The Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum and its Epicurean library
sources: Modern scholarly inference from the Villa of the Papyri; no ancient attestation

stops.name: Cremona, the fields given to the veterans
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the general historical record of the Philippi settlements
stops.campa: The triumvirs win at Philippi and owe their soldiers land. Italy has none spare, so it is taken: whole territories marked out and handed to discharged men who have been promised farms through eleven years of civil war. Cremona is on the list because Cremona backed the wrong side, and Cremona's fields do not suffice. The surveyors move east into the territory of Mantua. Virgil is twenty-eight, at Naples with his philosophers, and the country he grew up in is being measured out in squares by men with rods.
suggested_refs: The veteran land settlements of 42-41 BC in Cisalpine Gaul
sources: General Roman historical record of the Philippi land settlements

stops.name: Andes, the farm confiscated
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode is reconstructed from Eclogues 1 and 9, an autobiographical reading disputed by modern scholars
stops.campa: The family holding at Andes goes with the rest. A soldier takes the house, the woodland the father had bought, the hives. What is known of that day is known only because two poems say something like it: an old man driving his goats off ground that is no longer his, and another man watching a stranger's harvest come up in furrows he cut. Whether the shepherd Meliboeus is the poet's father is a question the poems do not answer and scholars have not stopped asking. The Life says it happened. The Life is three centuries late.
suggested_refs: Eclogues 1 and 9, the sole detailed evidence for the confiscation

stops.name: The Mincio, the swim
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; the aggressor is named Arrius in some manuscripts and Clodius in others
stops.campa: The later biographers add a scene the poems do not have. The veteran holding the farm comes at Virgil with a sword; the poet runs, goes into the river, and swims for the far bank. Some manuscripts call the man Arrius, others Clodius, and no source corroborates either. The river is the only witness and it says nothing. It comes out of Lake Garda, loops three times around the walls of Mantua, and goes down through the reeds to the Po, and those reeds keep turning up in other men's mouths all through the Eclogues.
suggested_refs: The scholia to Eclogue 9, which name the veteran differently in different manuscripts

stops.name: Rome, the patrons who do not agree
stops.date_confidence: the restitution is reported by several sources; which patron secured it is contradicted between them and left unresolved here
stops.campa: He goes up to Rome to ask for the land back and gets it, and at that point the record splits four ways. The Life of Donatus credits Octavian himself. Other accounts credit Asinius Pollio. Servius on the ninth eclogue brings in Cornelius Gallus and Alfenus Varus. Some modern readers doubt the farm ever came back at all. No source consulted here chooses between them. What the first eclogue says is that a god made this leisure, and that the god was a young man at Rome to whom the speaker went and by whom he was heard.
suggested_refs: Servius, commentary on Eclogues 9, and Donatus, Vita Vergilii 19-21, which do not agree

stops.name: Mantua, the ten pastorals
stops.date_confidence: composition dated c. 42 to 39 BC by ancient consensus and internal evidence; publication usually placed 39 to 38 BC and contested
stops.campa: Between the confiscations and the end of the decade he writes ten poems in the manner of Theocritus, and does to Sicilian shepherds what no Greek had thought to do: puts the eviction of Italian farmers into their singing matches. Tityrus keeps his fields. Meliboeus loses his and goes off to Africa or Scythia. Gods, slaves, and surveyors share a landscape that is supposed to hold nothing but goats and love complaints. The book is read aloud at Rome and performed on the stage by mimes, and a provincial nobody of thirty becomes the poet everyone has heard of.
suggested_refs: The Eclogues performed on the Roman stage by mimes, reported in the Life

stops.name: Rome, the fourth eclogue in Pollio's consulship
stops.date_confidence: dated by the poem's own reference to the consulship of Asinius Pollio
stops.campa: In the consulship of Pollio he writes a poem about a child soon to be born who will close the age of iron and open the age of gold, so that the earth yields without labor and the serpent dies. Whose child, the poem does not say, and no reader of his own century seems to have needed to ask. Three hundred years later Constantine reads it aloud to an assembly as a prophecy of Christ. The church keeps Virgil on the strength of this poem, and Dante inherits him from the church.
suggested_refs: Eclogue 4 and its Christian reception from Constantine's Oration to the Assembly of the Saints onward
sources: Virgil, Eclogue 4, dated by its reference to Pollio's consulship

stops.name: Rome, the Esquiline and the circle of Maecenas
stops.date_confidence: the friendship is attested; property or residence on the Esquiline is inferred from Horace and not stated by any ancient text
stops.campa: Maecenas, who handles for Octavian everything that is not war, keeps gardens on the Esquiline laid over the old burial pits, and gathers poets there. Virgil is in the circle by about this year, and it is Virgil who brings Horace into it, nine months after their first meeting, by Horace's own account. Varius Rufus is in the room too, and eighteen years from now Varius will be handed an unfinished epic and an imperial instruction about what to do with it. Ovid, a generation behind, will write only that he saw Virgil.
suggested_refs: The gardens of Maecenas on the Esquiline, over the puticuli

stops.name: Sinuessa, the three friends join the party
stops.date_confidence: attested; the year is secure, the day of the meeting is not recorded
stops.campa: Maecenas is going south on business of state, Horace is with him, and at the coast town on the border of Latium and Campania three men are waiting: Plotius, Varius, and Virgil. Horace sets down what he felt when he saw them coming, and that line is the only surviving sentence in which a friend of Virgil's says what it was like to have him for a friend. Eighteen years from now, two of these three will be the men Augustus orders to edit the dead man's book and publish it against his written wish.
stops.quote: The next day's sunrise brings great joy: since Plotius Varius, and Virgil, meet us at Sinuessa: no more Shining spirits did earth ever bear, and no one Could be more dearly attached to them than I.
stops.quote_source: Horace, Satires 1.5.39-44, trans. A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation
suggested_refs: The site of ancient Sinuessa in the comune of Sessa Aurunca, on the Via Appia

stops.name: Caudium, the flyting of the two buffoons
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Above the taverns of Caudium stands the villa of Cocceius, well stocked, and the party dines there. The entertainment is a quarrel between two hangers-on, Sarmentus the scurra and Messius Cicirrus, who abuse each other for twenty lines about a scarred forehead, a horse's look, a runaway slave's collar, while the table laughs. Horace writes the whole match down, insult by insult. Virgil is in the room and says nothing anybody records, which is what the sources do with him almost everywhere: present, named, and silent.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.51-70, the contest of Sarmentus and Messius Cicirrus

stops.name: Beneventum, the thrushes and the fire
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Beneventum the anxious host, working too hard over lean thrushes on a spit, lets the flame slip up the old kitchen wall and nearly burns the house down around his guests. The greedy diners and the frightened slaves are snatching dinner off the hearth while the roof smokes above them, and then the fire is beaten out and everyone sits down again. This is the only week of Virgil's life that anyone wrote down while it was happening, and what got written down was the kitchen catching fire.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.71-76

stops.name: Trivicum, the smoke of green wood
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rain drives them off the road into a farmhouse near Trivicum, and the hearth there is fed with wet branches, leaves and all, so the room fills with smoke and every man in it weeps without grief. Horace lies awake most of the night waiting for a girl who does not come, and admits it in the poem. Outside, the Apennine weather. Inside, the literary establishment of the Augustan age crying at a fire that will not draw, two hundred miles from Rome and a hundred and fifty from the sea they are walking toward.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.79-85, the smoky villa near Trivicum, modern Trevico

stops.name: Canusium, the gritty bread
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Canusium's bread has grit in it, and the town keeps water by the jarful and no more, and Horace can find nothing else to say for the place except that valiant Diomedes founded it long ago. Varius leaves the company here and his friends part from him weeping. The stage survives because one poet in the party decided to make a poem out of the road itself, town by town and meal by meal. Another poet in the same party keeps quiet, and will make his poem out of a voyage.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.87-93, and the departure of Varius at Canusium

stops.name: Barium, the fishing town on the Adriatic
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Worn out by a long haul over bad roads made worse by rain, they come through Rubi footsore and then down to Barium on the sea, which Horace notes for its fish and for nothing else at all. The coast road runs flat and bright along the Adriatic from here. Horace, Virgil, and Plotius are in the carriages as ordinary passengers, complaining about the food and the state of the road. The Georgics are not begun. The Aeneid is eight years off and nobody in the party has heard of it.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.94-97, Rubi and Barium

stops.name: Egnatia, the incense that lights itself
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Egnatia the townsmen show the travellers a marvel: incense laid on the temple threshold catches and burns with no flame put to it. Horace refuses the miracle flatly and in verse, saying the gods live free of care and do not lean down out of the roof of heaven to do tricks for a coast town. Virgil, who has spent years under an Epicurean master teaching precisely that, is standing next to him and is not recorded as saying anything. Neither of them buys it. The town keeps the marvel anyway.
suggested_refs: Horace, Satires 1.5.97-104, the incense of Egnatia

stops.name: Brundisium, the end of the road and the page
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the journey occupies some fifteen days of travel
stops.campa: Brundisium is the end of the long road and the long page alike, and Horace closes the poem on that pun and stops. The port is where Italy runs out and the crossing to Greece begins: the columns on the quay, a harbour thick with grain ships and transports, the road behind them measured off in bad inns. Virgil walks out of the page here, and the record loses sight of his movements for the next eight years. He will come back to this harbour once more, at fifty, and will not leave it.
suggested_refs: The terminal columns of the Via Appia on the Brundisium quay

stops.name: Naples, the four books on the land
stops.date_confidence: composed c. 37 to 29 BC; the midpoint is pinned here
stops.campa: Seven years for two thousand lines: field crops, vines and olives, herds, and bees. He works, the Life says, by dictating a great many verses in the morning and then spending the rest of the day cutting them back, the way a bear licks a cub into shape. The subject is Italian dirt, in a decade when Italian dirt has been confiscated, fought over, and left to weeds. The book is dedicated to Maecenas. It ends with a swarm of bees generated out of a dead bullock, and with the poet naming himself, idle at Naples, while Caesar thunders on the Euphrates.
suggested_refs: Georgics 4.559-566, the poet's signature: illo Vergilium me tempore dulcis alebat Parthenope

stops.name: Nola, the water refused
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Aulus Gellius reports the anecdote and says himself that he does not know whether it is true
stops.campa: Aulus Gellius passes on a story he is not sure of. Virgil asks the town of Nola to run their water to an estate of his nearby; the Nolans refuse; and he strikes their name out of the finished poem, so that where the line had said Nola it now says ora, the coast, and the town is deleted from the Georgics for the length of Latin literature. No manuscript preserves the reading he is supposed to have cut. The line as it stands praises rich Capua and the country under the ridge of Vesuvius, and does not mention Nola at all.
suggested_refs: Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 6.20, on Georgics 2.224-225

stops.name: Atella, the Georgics read to Caesar over four days
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Octavian is coming home from Actium and Egypt with the world in his hand, and halts in Campania at Atella to rest his throat. For four days running Virgil reads him the Georgics, all four books in order, and when the poet's voice gives out Maecenas takes the scroll and reads on from where he stopped. It happens in a small town off the road, in a sickroom, out loud, to an audience of one man and whoever is standing at the door. Nothing is said about what the audience thought.
suggested_refs: Donatus, Vita Vergilii 27, the four-day recitation at Atella

stops.name: Naples, the eleven years
stops.date_confidence: composition c. 29 to 19 BC, attested by the Life and by Propertius's allusion to the poem in progress
stops.campa: He takes up an epic about a Trojan who left a burning city and founded a people in Latium, and it holds him until he dies. He drafts the whole thing in prose first, cuts it into twelve books, and versifies whatever part he pleases in no order at all. Where a line will not come he sets down half of one and leaves it standing, a prop under the building, meaning to return. Aeneas walks every stage of that route, and Dido burns at Carthage, because these are the sentences he is making here at Naples.
stops.quote: Can heav'nly minds such high resentment show, Or exercise their spite in human woe?
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid I, trans. John Dryden, Project Gutenberg ed. 228
suggested_refs: The tibicines, unfinished half-lines left standing in the published Aeneid

stops.name: Cumae, the mouth of the cave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no ancient source records a visit, which is inferred from the poem's topographic precision
stops.campa: An hour up the coast from where he is writing, the rock at Cumae is cut with a hundred mouths, and the Sibyl's answer comes out of all of them at once. Below it lies Avernus, the lake whose birds are said not to fly over. Book six sends Aeneas down here with a golden bough to speak to his father among the dead. Whether Virgil walked this ground himself, no source says; the geography in the poem is exact enough that scholars assume he did, and the assumption is all that survives to go on.
stops.quote: the path to hell is easy: black Dis's door is open night and day: but to retrace your steps, and go out to the air above, that is work, that is the task.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid VI, trans. A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation
suggested_refs: The Antro della Sibilla at Cumae and the shore of Lake Avernus

stops.name: Rome, the Palatine and the reading of the sixth book
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the fainting and the payment per verse are treated by many scholars as embellishment on a historical reading
stops.campa: In the house on the Palatine he reads three books aloud to Augustus and to Octavia: the second, the fourth, and the sixth. The fourth is Dido, whose Carthage tradition places on Byrsa hill on the strength of these lines. In the sixth, among the souls not yet born, a young man walks under a black cloud and the poet names him: you shall be Marcellus. Octavia, whose son Marcellus died at Baiae this year at nineteen, faints in the room. She is said to have paid ten thousand sesterces for each of the lines.
stops.quote: Give way you Roman authors! Give way you Greeks! Something more than the Iliad's being born.
stops.quote_source: Propertius, Elegies 2.34, trans. A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation
suggested_refs: Aeneid 6.860-886, the Marcellus passage

stops.name: Athens, the emperor met on the way out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the dating of Horace's propempticon to this particular crossing is not established
stops.campa: At fifty he sails east, meaning to spend three years in Greece and Asia doing nothing but revising the poem, and then to give whatever remains of his life to philosophy. At Athens he meets Augustus coming back from the East, and gives the plan up: he will go home with the imperial party instead. Horace had once written a poem for a ship carrying Virgil to Athens, asking the winds and the goddess of Cyprus to deliver their cargo whole, and calling that cargo half of his own soul.
stops.quote: bring him safely there I beg you, and there watch over half of my spirit.
stops.quote_source: Horace, Odes 1.3, trans. A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation
suggested_refs: Horace, Odes 1.3, the propempticon for the ship carrying Virgil

stops.name: Megara, the sun and the fever
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Life; the month is inferred from the death date and the length of the crossing
stops.campa: Waiting on the emperor's movements he crosses over to look at Megara, a ruined town in a hot country, and walks the site under a fierce sun. He is ill by the time he comes back. He boards for Italy already weakened, and the crossing makes it worse day after day, the fever climbing while the coast of Greece falls behind. In his baggage are twelve books nobody else has read entire, fifty-odd lines of which stop in the middle, and the three years he had set aside to finish them are now not going to happen.
suggested_refs: Donatus, Vita Vergilii 35, the illness contracted at Megara

stops.name: Brundisium, the death and the book boxes
stops.date_confidence: attested; the deathbed request to burn the poem is tradition and its authenticity is disputed
stops.campa: The fleet lands at Brundisium and he dies there a few days after, on the twenty-first of September, in his fifty-first year. Before sailing he had asked Varius to burn the Aeneid if anything happened to him, and Varius had refused. Now he calls for the book boxes so as to do it himself, and nobody brings them to the bed. Cicero, dead twenty-four years, had turned three times at this same port: out into exile, back from exile, and into Caesar's pardon. Virgil reaches it once and does not leave.
stops.quote: he had given instructions that the Aeneid should be burned
stops.quote_source: Aelius Donatus, Vita Vergilii, and Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights
suggested_refs: The Roman house at Brindisi shown since the Middle Ages as the place of Virgil's death

stops.name: Rome, Augustus orders the poem published
stops.date_confidence: the instruction is attested; publication is placed at 19 BC or shortly after, and the 17 BC date sometimes given has no ancient support
stops.campa: Augustus overrides the dead man's wish and hands the manuscript to Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca with one instruction: correct, take nothing away, add nothing. So the poem goes out with its scaffolding still standing, the half-lines stopping where he left them, and an ending in which the hero kills a man begging for mercy and the book simply stops. Ovid, twenty-four that year and about to inherit the language, will write later that of that generation he saw Virgil and no more than saw him.
stops.quote: Virgil I only saw: and greedy fate granted Tibullus no time for my friendship.
stops.quote_source: Ovid, Tristia 4.10, trans. A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation
suggested_refs: The editorial commission of Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca

stops.name: Naples, the tomb on the road to Puteoli
stops.date_confidence: burial near Naples on the Puteoli road is attested in antiquity; the structure shown today is a later identification that cannot be confirmed
stops.campa: His bones are carried from Brundisium to Naples at his own wish and buried beside the road to Puteoli at the second milestone, at the mouth of the tunnel cut through the hill of Posillipo. The couplet they set up says Mantua bore him, Calabria took him, Parthenope holds him now, and that he sang pastures, farms, and leaders, which is his three books in the order he wrote them. Eighteen centuries later Giambattista Vico will spend his entire working life in this city and be buried in it too.
stops.quote: Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope: cecini pascua, rura, duces.
stops.quote_source: Epitaph attributed to Virgil, transmitted via Aelius Donatus, Vita Vergilii
suggested_refs: The columbarium tomb in the Parco Vergiliano a Piedigrotta, at the entrance to the Crypta Neapolitana

stops.name: Vatican, two illustrated codices out of three
stops.date_confidence: the Vergilius Vaticanus is dated c. 400 CE and the Vergilius Romanus c. 480 to 490 CE
stops.campa: Of the three illustrated manuscripts of classical literature that survive from antiquity, two are Virgil. The Vergilius Vaticanus, painted at Rome around the year four hundred, and the Vergilius Romanus, eighty years after it, end on the same shelf in the Vatican Library. The third is a Homer. Nobody made a picture book of Ennius or of Lucan. The empire coming apart around these painters spends its remaining money copying out, with illustrations, the poem about how it was founded.
suggested_refs: Vergilius Vaticanus (Vat. lat. 3225) and Vergilius Romanus (Vat. lat. 3867), Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana

stops.name: Naples, the bronze fly and the magician
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the earliest secure witnesses are Alexander Neckam c. 1190, Conrad of Querfurt 1194, and Gervase of Tilbury 1214, not the Policraticus as is sometimes claimed
stops.campa: Twelve hundred years after they buried him here, the city has turned him into a sorcerer. Conrad of Querfurt writes home that Virgil built a bronze fly and set it over a gate, and no fly entered Naples afterward, and the plague stopped; that he laid an egg in the foundation of a castle and the castle stands on it still; that he made a head of brass that spoke. Alexander Neckam and Gervase of Tilbury carry the same tales. This Virgil has no Latin in him. He is a civic protector, and he comes before Dante's.
suggested_refs: Conrad of Querfurt's letter of 1194 and Gervase of Tilbury, Otia Imperialia (1214)
sources: Comparetti, Vergil in the Middle Ages (via secondary summary)

stops.name: Limbo, the castle of the unbaptized wise
stops.date_confidence: the pin follows the poem's own cosmology, which sinks the funnel of Hell directly beneath the hill of the crucifixion
stops.campa: In the Easter of the jubilee year a Florentine lost in a dark wood meets a shade who names himself, and the shade is Virgil, sent down by three women in heaven to bring him through. In the first circle, behind a wall and inside a green meadow, stands the castle where Homer, Horace, Ovid, and Lucan sit with Aristotle and Plato, and this is the guide's own eternal address, the place he must come back to. He leads Dante through every gate in the poem except the last one, and then goes home to it.
stops.quote: Now not man, man once I was, And born of Lombard parents, Mantuana both By country, when the power of Julius yet Was scarcely firm.
stops.quote_source: Dante Alighieri, Inferno I, trans. Henry Francis Cary, Project Gutenberg ed. 8800
suggested_refs: Inferno IV, the noble castle of the virtuous pagans

stops.name: Ravenna, the Latin eclogues to Giovanni del Virgilio
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A Bolognese teacher whose own byname is Giovanni del Virgilio writes to Dante in exile, urging him to drop the vulgar tongue and write in the tongue of Virgil, and dangling the laurel crown for it. Dante answers in Latin hexameters, two pastoral eclogues composed in the manner of Virgil's own, and goes on writing the Commedia in Italian regardless. The guide is being used, at that particular moment, as the argument against the poem he is a character in.
stops.quote: And art thou then that Virgil, that well-spring, From which such copious floods of eloquence Have issued?
stops.quote_source: Dante Alighieri, Inferno I, trans. Henry Francis Cary, Project Gutenberg ed. 8800
suggested_refs: The Latin eclogues exchanged between Dante and Giovanni del Virgilio, 1319-1320

stops.name: Milan, Petrarch's Virgil in the Ambrosiana
stops.date_confidence: the frontispiece is dated c. 1336 and was painted at Avignon; this pin marks where the codex is kept now, not where it was made
stops.campa: Petrarch owns a Virgil and writes in its margins his whole life, including the note in which he records the death of Laura. For the front of it he has Simone Martini paint, at Avignon, a scene in which Servius the commentator draws back a curtain on the poet lying under a tree with his pen lifted, while Aeneas stands armed on one side and a farmer prunes a vine on the other: the three books in one picture, with the scholar holding the cloth aside so that the reader can see in. The volume is in Milan now.
suggested_refs: The Ambrosian Virgil (Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS A 79 inf.) with Simone Martini's frontispiece
sources: Established art-historical record of the Ambrosian Virgil

stops.name: Rome, the first printed Virgil
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, two Germans working a press in Rome, put the collected works through it: Eclogues, Georgics, Aeneid, the editio princeps, within two decades of Gutenberg. Copying by hand does not stop for another generation, and the early printed text is worse than the best manuscripts. What changes is the arithmetic. A book that had cost a scribe most of a year now comes off the forme three hundred times over, and the price of owning Virgil falls to something a schoolmaster can pay.
suggested_refs: The 1469 Rome editio princeps of Virgil, printed by Sweynheym and Pannartz
sources: Standard incunabula record; the Rylands blog cited in gathering returns 404 and is not used

stops.name: Venice, the Aldine italic
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Aldus Manutius prints a Virgil at Venice in a new cursive letter cut for him by Francesco Griffo, in a format small enough to hold in one hand and cheap enough to own: the first of the octavo classics, a book for the pocket rather than the lectern. Italic type enters European printing carrying this poem. Nine years later Giulio Camillo takes lodgings in San Polo beside that press, in a city where the Aldine Aristotle and the Aldine Virgil are already in the hands of half of literate Europe.
suggested_refs: The Aldine Virgil of 1501, first book set in Griffo's italic
sources: Standard history of the Aldine press

stops.name: London, Dryden's Virgil
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: John Dryden, old, out of favour at court since the revolution, and stripped of the laureateship for refusing the oath, translates the whole of Virgil by public subscription and brings it out in one folio with plates. For the next century and a half this is what Virgil says in English, in heroic couplets, to readers who will never construe a line of the Latin. Subscribers pay five guineas to have their coats of arms printed under the engravings. The opening three words are the three everybody knows.
stops.quote: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc'd by fate, And haughty Juno's unrelenting hate, Expell'd and exil'd, left the Trojan shore.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid I, trans. John Dryden, Project Gutenberg ed. 228
suggested_refs: The Works of Virgil (London, 1697), Dryden's subscription folio
sources: Standard literary-historical record of Dryden's Works of Virgil

stops.name: Fountain Court, the Strand: Blake draws the guide
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: John Linnell commissions a set of Divine Comedy watercolours from William Blake, who is sixty-seven, poor, working in two rooms off the Strand, and reads no Italian, so he goes at it with a borrowed English translation and a dictionary. Among the hundred-odd sheets left unfinished when he dies are Dante and Virgil among the ice of Cocytus and the pair of them in the whirlwind of the lustful. The Mantuan is drawn from behind, robed, one arm out, pointing at whatever the pilgrim is being made to look at.
suggested_refs: Blake's Dante watercolours of 1824-1827, including 'Dante and Virgil among the ice'

stops.name: Palais Garnier, Dante and Virgil on the operatic stage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ambroise Thomas's Françoise de Rimini opens at the Paris Opera with a prologue Paul Barbier has cut out of the fifth canto of the Inferno: the pilgrim Dante and his guide Virgil go down into the second circle, where the wind never rests, and Francesca tells them how she and Paolo came to be in it. Then the opera proper begins and the two poets stand aside. A Roman dead nineteen centuries takes a supporting part, in a costume some Paris workshop has guessed at, in a love story about a book.
suggested_refs: Françoise de Rimini, libretto by Barbier and Carré, Palais Garnier, 14 April 1882

stops.name: London, the classic of all Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the exact date of the Virgil Society lecture is not established in the sources reached
stops.campa: In the last winter of the war, with the city bombed flat in places and the Virgil Society meeting anyway, T. S. Eliot stands up to ask what a classic is and answers with one name. Not Homer, whom the Romantics had preferred; Virgil, on the grounds of maturity of mind, maturity of manners, maturity of language, and a common style. Europe is in pieces outside the hall. The poem he is proposing at its centre was written to explain to one empire, in twelve books, why it deserved to exist.
suggested_refs: T. S. Eliot, 'What Is a Classic?', address to the Virgil Society, 1944
sources: Established literary-historical record of Eliot's 1944 Virgil Society lecture
